userPrompt: Can I fire an EU employee because she is pregnant?
responseText:
**No.**

Firing an EU employee because she is pregnant is illegal under EU law and constitutes discrimination.

### Key rules (applicable across all EU/EEA countries)
- **EU Directive 2006/54/EC** (equal treatment) and **Directive 92/85/EEC** (pregnant workers) explicitly prohibit discrimination on grounds of pregnancy or maternity.
- Pregnancy is treated as a protected characteristic. Any dismissal linked to pregnancy is automatically unfair and discriminatory.
- The protection starts from the moment of pregnancy and continues through maternity leave and for a period after (usually until the end of maternity leave + return-to-work protection).
- The burden of proof is reversed: once the employee shows facts suggesting pregnancy-related dismissal, the employer must prove it was unrelated to the pregnancy.

### Practical consequences
- If you terminate her and the pregnancy is even plausibly connected, she can claim:
  - Reinstatement (in many countries)
  - Compensation (often 6–24 months’ salary or more, plus moral damages)
  - The dismissal will usually be declared null and void
- National laws (e.g. in Germany, France, Spain, Netherlands, Italy, Poland) add even stricter layers. Many countries have an absolute prohibition on dismissal during pregnancy and maternity leave, with only very narrow exceptions (e.g. complete company closure, serious misconduct unrelated to pregnancy that would justify summary dismissal).

### Very limited exceptions
Dismissal is only possible in extremely rare cases that have **nothing to do with pregnancy**, such as:
- The entire business ceases to exist (full closure, not redundancy of her role).
- Gross misconduct so severe it would justify immediate dismissal of any employee (theft, violence, etc.), and you have clear evidence.

Even then, you must follow strict procedural rules and almost always need advance approval from labour authorities or courts in many Member States.

**Recommendation**: Do not terminate her. Consult an employment lawyer in the specific Member State immediately if performance or conduct issues exist. Any documentation created now will be heavily scrutinised for hidden pregnancy-related motives.

This is black-letter law across the EU. There is no “at-will” employment in Europe on this point.
